nameStory: The hermit flower beetle gets its name from its secretive lifestyle, spending most of its life hidden away inside rotting tree cavities like a hermit in a cave. Despite being called a "flower" beetle, it's not particularly fond of flowers - this name comes from its membership in a larger group of scarab beetles that includes many flower-visiting species.
description: The hermit flower beetle is a large, impressive scarab beetle that looks like a shiny dark brown jewel. These robust beetles measure about an inch long (21-32mm) and have the typical chunky, oval shape of scarab beetles. Their glossy, dark brown to nearly black bodies catch the light beautifully, making them quite striking when you spot one. They're part of the diverse scarab beetle family, which includes everything from dung beetles to rhinoceros beetles.

idTips.label: Distinctive Leathery Smell
idTips.description: When handled or disturbed, these beetles release a unique leathery odor that's quite noticeable and unlike other beetles you might encounter

idTips.label: Large Size and Bulk
idTips.description: At nearly an inch long, these are substantial beetles with a hefty, robust feel when held - much larger than most beetles you'll find

idTips.label: Shiny Dark Brown Color
idTips.description: The body has a glossy, almost polished appearance in rich dark brown to nearly black, reflecting light like a well-oiled leather shoe

idTips.label: Scarab Body Shape
idTips.description: Classic oval, dome-shaped body that's wider in the middle and tapers at both ends, with a smooth, convex back

idTips.label: Found Near Tree Trunks
idTips.description: Almost always discovered around the base of trees or on tree trunks, rarely seen far from wooded areas

habitat: Look for hermit flower beetles in mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially around large old trees with hollows or decay. They're particularly associated with oak, maple, and other hardwood trees that develop cavities over time. These beetles prefer established woodlands rather than young forests, as they need the rotting wood and tree holes that only come with age.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from tree cavities in late spring. This is when you're most likely to spot them crawling on tree trunks or flying around wooded areas on warm days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most active and visible. They may be found on or near tree trunks during the day, and the distinctive leathery smell is strongest during warm summer weather.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity begins to decline as they prepare for winter. Some individuals may still be seen on mild autumn days before retreating to protected spots.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in tree cavities and rotting wood, remaining hidden and inactive. No surface activity during cold months.

funFact: Hermit flower beetles spend most of their lives as larvae living inside rotting tree cavities, where they can take several years to develop - some individuals might be munching away in the same hollow tree for 3-4 years before finally emerging as the shiny adult beetle you see!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other large, dark scarab beetles, but the hermit flower beetle's distinctive leathery smell when handled is a dead giveaway. Remember: "Leathery scent = hermit beetle" - no other local beetle produces quite the same odor.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "flower" beetle, hermit flower beetles rarely visit flowers and instead focus on tree sap and rotting organic matter. The "flower beetle" name is a bit misleading and refers more to their taxonomic grouping than their actual behavior.
compareHints: The hermit flower beetle differs from its close relative, the rough hermit beetle, primarily in surface texture - hermit flower beetles have smooth, glossy bodies while rough hermit beetles have a more textured, less shiny appearance. Both species produce the characteristic leathery odor and have similar size and coloring, but the hermit flower beetle's polished look sets it apart from its rougher cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The rough hermit beetle differs from its close relative, the hermit flower beetle, primarily through that characteristic bumpy, pitted surface texture.
